stem: Which wireless technology is most often used to link a phone to wireless earphones?

options.content: Bluetooth
options.rationale: Correct: low-power, short-range links between nearby devices.

options.content: WiMAX
options.rationale: WiMAX is wireless broadband over kilometres.

options.content: Microwave
options.rationale: Microwave links join towers or satellites.

options.content: Satellite
options.rationale: Satellites relay signals over very long distances.

explanation: Bluetooth is designed for short-range, low-power connections such as earphones, keyboards and car kits.

stem: Why does a TV remote control that uses infra-red stop working when someone stands between it and the television?

options.content: Infra-red needs a clear line of sight
options.rationale: Correct: the person blocks the infra-red beam.

options.content: Infra-red signals pass through people but not furniture
options.rationale: Infra-red is blocked by any solid object.

options.content: The remote and TV must be paired again
options.rationale: Pairing is a Bluetooth feature.

options.content: Infra-red only works over several kilometres
options.rationale: Infra-red works over only a few metres.

explanation: Infra-red travels in straight lines and is blocked by solid objects, so the sender must 'see' the receiver.

stem: What is the main difference between Wi-Fi and WiMAX?

options.content: Wi-Fi uses cables; WiMAX is wireless
options.rationale: Both are wireless.

options.content: WiMAX covers kilometres; Wi-Fi covers tens of metres
options.rationale: Correct: WiMAX is wide-area wireless broadband.

options.content: WiMAX is only for TV remote controls
options.rationale: That is infra-red.

options.content: Wi-Fi needs a line of sight; WiMAX does not
options.rationale: Wi-Fi does not need a line of sight.

explanation: Wi-Fi provides a wireless LAN within a building; WiMAX provides wireless broadband over a much larger area.

stem: How does a GPS receiver in a phone work out its position?

options.content: By asking the nearest Wi-Fi access point for a map
options.rationale: GPS uses satellites, not Wi-Fi.

options.content: From an infra-red beam sent by a tower
options.rationale: Infra-red works only over a few metres.

options.content: From signals received from several satellites
options.rationale: Correct: it uses timing signals from navigation satellites.

options.content: By pairing with other phones nearby using Bluetooth
options.rationale: Bluetooth does not provide location.

explanation: A GPS receiver calculates its position from the signals of several navigation satellites.

stem: A telecoms company joins two masts on hilltops 30 km apart with dishes pointing at each other. Which technology is it using?

options.content: Bluetooth
options.rationale: Bluetooth reaches about 10 m.

options.content: Infra-red
options.rationale: Infra-red reaches only a few metres.

options.content: Wi-Fi
options.rationale: Wi-Fi covers tens of metres from an access point.

options.content: Microwave
options.rationale: Correct: point-to-point microwave links need line of sight between dishes.

explanation: Microwave links carry data between towers tens of kilometres apart, as long as the dishes have a line of sight.
hints: The link must cover a long distance between two fixed points that can see each other.

stem: Why are radio waves used for broadcasting to thousands of listeners?

options.content: They need a direct line of sight to each radio
options.rationale: That is true of infra-red and microwave, not broadcast radio.

options.content: They can only travel a few metres, so they are private
options.rationale: Radio waves travel long distances.

options.content: Each radio must be paired with the transmitter first
options.rationale: Pairing is a Bluetooth feature.

options.content: They spread out over long distances and pass through walls
options.rationale: Correct: one transmitter reaches many receivers.

explanation: Radio waves travel far and pass through buildings, so one transmitter can serve a whole region.
hints: Which waves pass through walls and spread out from one transmitter?

stem: Which is a **disadvantage** of satellite internet for a remote school?

options.content: It can only be used within a few metres of the satellite
options.rationale: Satellites cover huge areas.

options.content: It needs a cable laid all the way from the school to the nearest town
options.rationale: Satellite links need no cable to town.

options.content: A delay, because signals travel a very long way to the satellite and back
options.rationale: Correct: the long path causes noticeable delay.

options.content: It works only with infra-red devices
options.rationale: Satellite equipment uses microwaves.

explanation: Satellite links reach remote places but are costly, add delay and can be disrupted by heavy storms.
hints: Think about distance travelled by the signal.

stem: An internet provider wants to give broadband to 200 homes in a village 5 km from its nearest tower, without laying cables. Which technology is most suitable?

options.content: Wi-Fi from one access point
options.rationale: One Wi-Fi access point covers only tens of metres.

options.content: Bluetooth
options.rationale: Bluetooth reaches about 10 m.

options.content: WiMAX
options.rationale: Correct: wide-area wireless broadband over several kilometres.

options.content: Infra-red
options.rationale: Infra-red needs line of sight and reaches a few metres.

explanation: WiMAX base stations serve homes kilometres away, so it suits wireless broadband to a village.
hints: The village is several kilometres from the provider and has no cables.

stem: Two Bluetooth devices must usually be paired before they can exchange data.
explanation: True. Pairing links the two devices so that only they exchange data.

stem: Infra-red signals can pass through walls, so a remote control works from another room.
explanation: False. Infra-red is blocked by walls and needs a line of sight.

stem: Match each use to the most suitable wireless technology.

left.content: Connecting laptops to the internet in a school library
A hands-free kit linking a phone to a car's speakers

explanation: Library: Wi-Fi. Car kit: Bluetooth. Remote control: infra-red. Broadcasting: radio waves.

stem: Match each mobile technology to a role it plays in communication.

right.content: Relays television and internet to remote areas
Voice calls, messaging and mobile money from almost anywhere
Larger touch screen for e-learning and video calls

explanation: Each device's role follows from its size and connections; satellites relay signals over long distances.

payload.template: Bluetooth has a range of about {{blank:a}}. Wi-Fi devices connect to a wireless {{blank:b}} point. Microwave and infra-red links both need a clear line of {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Bluetooth: about 10 m. Wi-Fi: wireless access point. Microwave and infra-red: line of sight.

stem: Name the wireless technology used by most television remote controls.
explanation: Most remote controls send infra-red pulses to the television.

stem: Describe **two** ways in which mobile phones have improved communication for people in rural Zimbabwe.

points.description: People can call or message family, clinics or buyers without travelling / from almost anywhere with coverage
Mobile money and mobile data give access to banking, market prices, weather or e-learning without visiting a town

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A farmer can phone a buyer or a vet instead of travelling to town, and can use mobile money to pay suppliers and receive payments without a bank branch nearby.

explanation: Mobile phones bring calls, messaging, banking and information to places without landlines or banks.
hints: Think of banking and of reaching people in rural areas.

stem: A conservation team works in a remote part of Gonarezhou with no mobile signal. Explain why it might use satellite communication, and give **one** drawback.

points.description: Satellites cover remote areas where there are no masts or cables
so the team can make calls / send data / use GPS from anywhere in the park
Drawback: expensive equipment and airtime / signal delay / disrupted by storms or blocked by thick trees

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A satellite phone works anywhere under the satellite's coverage, with no need for a mast, so rangers can report sightings and emergencies from deep in the park. However, satellite equipment and calls are expensive.

explanation: Satellites reach anywhere under their coverage, at a cost in money and delay.

stem: Thandeka runs a guest house in Kariba. She wants guests to use the internet in their rooms, a wireless speaker in the lounge and a link to the internet provider's tower 8 km away.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which technology should give guests internet access in their rooms?

options.content: Infra-red
options.rationale: Needs line of sight and reaches a few metres.

options.content: Wi-Fi
options.rationale: Correct: a wireless LAN covering the building.

options.content: Bluetooth
options.rationale: Too short a range for a whole guest house.

options.content: Satellite TV
options.rationale: Satellite TV broadcasts television; it is not the guest house's local network.

parts.explanation: Wi-Fi provides wireless access within a building.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name a wireless technology that could link the guest house to the provider's tower 8 km away.
parts.explanation: WiMAX or a microwave link both cover several kilometres.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why Bluetooth is suitable for the wireless speaker in the lounge.

points.description: The speaker is close to the phone/device, within Bluetooth's short range (about 10 m)
Bluetooth uses little power / devices pair easily without a network

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The guest's phone is only a few metres from the speaker, within Bluetooth's range, and Bluetooth uses little power and pairs directly without needing the Wi-Fi network.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Guests in the far rooms complain that Wi-Fi is slow. Suggest **two** reasons.

points.description: The signal weakens with distance and thick walls
The bandwidth is shared between many users / interference from other devices

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The far rooms are a long way from the access point and the signal passes through thick walls, and many guests are sharing the same bandwidth at once.

hints: Match range to the distance in each situation.
Pairing and low power are Bluetooth features.

stem: An agricultural extension service in Masvingo province gives its field officers tablets with mobile data.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: A tablet with mobile data connects to the internet through the mobile network's masts (base stations).
parts.explanation: True. Mobile data uses the masts of the mobile network.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Match each task the officers do to the technology that supports it.

left.content: Recording the exact location of a field
Sending a report to head office from a farm
Printing at the district office without cables

parts.explanation: GPS gives location, mobile data works in the field, Wi-Fi serves the office LAN.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of giving the officers tablets instead of paper forms.

points.description: Benefit: data is sent to head office immediately, so advice and decisions are faster
Benefit: photos, GPS location and video lessons can be shared with farmers
Drawback: no coverage in some rural areas / cost of data
Drawback: limited battery life / tablets can be lost, stolen or damaged with personal data on them

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Reports and photos reach head office the moment they are taken, and officers can show farmers training videos and record field locations by GPS. However, some farms have no coverage, data costs money, batteries run down on long trips, and a lost tablet could expose farmers' details.

hints: Mobile networks use masts serving cells.
Weigh benefits against limits such as battery and coverage.
